Thanks for the clarification — I agree that this is counterintuitive.

The compiler currently treats the function identities themselves as the
safe memoization boundary. In your example, it can’t assume that
"cheapFunction()" is independent of "cheapFunction"’s identity, so when
that identity changes it conservatively recomputes the whole expression.
The "useMemo" version gives the compiler an explicit boundary, which is why
it can split the work into two memoized steps.

So yes, removing "useMemo" can change the generated memoization strategy
today, and that’s a limitation of the compiler rather than something you
should have to reason about from the output in every case. If you have a
reduced repro where the compiler is missing an optimization it should
preserve, please share it — otherwise the safest guidance for now is to
keep the explicit memoization where that boundary matters.

On Tue, Jun 23, 2026, 12:01 AM droooney ***@***.***> wrote:

> *droooney* left a comment (react/react#36848)
> <https://github.com/react/react/issues/36848#issuecomment-4775740492>
>
> Has explicit call out of dependencies (that is, suboptimal), so the React
> compiler will respect those memo hints.
>
> But it is not suboptimal. In Example 1, expensiveFunction gets called
> each time cheapFunction changes even if the result of cheapFunction()
> doesn't change, which is not desirable considering their names.
>
> The point though is more about how the logic changes once I remove useMemo
> from my code, which is extremely counterintuitive. How am I to get rid of
> useMemo / useCallback if I need to take a deep dive in the compiler in
> each case (and the case from the example is oversimplified, in reality
> there are way more dependencies and calls which are hard to trace in the
> output)?
